assignmentHtml.task:
核查关于DART的主张C1和C2。

起点：https://science.nasa.gov/mission/dart/

关键问题：

  1. DART是否在2022年9月撞击了Didymos（主小行星）？
  2. 轨道周期缩短了多少？是否约为33分钟？确切数值是否为33分15秒？这一结果首次公布与论文发表分别是什么时候？
  3. “动能撞击偏转效果”究竟证实了什么？能否将其推广为“任何危险小行星，无论其大小、结构或预警时间如何”？
  4. 后续相互绕行轨道的估计结果与日心轨道结果分别是什么？不要混淆这些量。

查找《Science》论文、NASA公告及后续分析。
assignmentHtml.context: 任务：DART（Double Asteroid Redirection Test，双小行星重定向测试）。目标：Dimorphos–Didymos双小行星系统。主张C1—C2：C1称DART撞击了主星Didymos，并使绕太阳运行的轨道周期缩短约33分钟，且首次公告给出的确切数值为33分15秒。C2称该实验证实了动能撞击偏转，因此任何危险小行星都能被化险为夷，无论其大小、结构或预警时间如何。这些是待核查的主张。注意：DART实际撞击的是Dimorphos（小卫星/次星），而非Didymos（主星）。
assignmentHtml.expected_output: 对C1和C2的每个组成部分给出判定，附修正后的文本、确切日期、带单位的周期变化数值、不确定性、相互绕行轨道与日心轨道结果的区别，以及结论的推广限制。必须提供来源URL。

answerHtml:
C1 and C2 each contain critical factual errors and overgeneralizations. Below is a component-by-component audit.

C1 AUDIT

C1a. "DART hit Didymos (the primary asteroid)" → FALSE

DART struck Dimorphos, the smaller moonlet (~160 m / 530 ft diameter), not Didymos, the larger primary (~780 m / 2,560 ft diameter). NASA's own mission page states: "On Sept. 26, 2022, DART impacted the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos... It orbits a larger, 2,560-foot (780-meter) asteroid called Didymos." NASA DART page; JHU APL release.

C1b. "Shortened solar orbital period by ~33 min" → INCORRECT: two distinct orbital quantities conflated

The ~33-minute change applies to the mutual orbit — Dimorphos's period orbiting Didymos — NOT to the heliocentric (solar) orbital period. The heliocentric effect is entirely different: the Didymos–Dimorphos binary system's orbit around the Sun changed by only ~0.15 seconds in period (−150 ± 20 ms) and −11.7 ± 1.3 micrometers/second in along-track velocity Makadia et al., Science Advances (2026). NASA explicitly notes this tiny heliocentric change demonstrates that even a small deflection accumulates over time: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/dart/nasas-dart-mission-changed-orbit-of-asteroid-didymos-around-sun/.

C1c. "Exact value 33 minutes 15 seconds as first-announcement value" → FALSE timeline

Three distinct measured values at three dates:

  • Oct 11, 2022 (first NASA confirmation, Release 22-105): ~32 minutes (±2 min uncertainty), shortened from 11h 55min to 11h 23min. Source: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-confirms-dart-mission-impact-changed-asteroids-motion-in-space/
  • Mar 1, 2023 (Thomas et al., Nature 616, 448–451): −33.0 ± 1.0 min (3σ); pre-impact period 11.92148 ± 0.00013 h; post-impact 11.372 ± 0.017 h. Two independent methods agreed. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05805-2
  • Mar 2024 (Naidu et al., Planetary Science Journal): refined to an immediate post-impact shortening of 32 min 42 s, settling after weeks of mass loss to a final shortening of 33 min 15 s (±1.5 s accuracy), with final period 11h 22m 3s. This is the source of the "33 min 15 s" figure. Source: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-study-asteroids-orbit-shape-changed-after-dart-impact/

"33 min 15 s" is the latest refined value from March 2024, not the first-announcement value.

C1d. Pre-impact period discrepancy

The Nature paper reports a pre-impact period of 11.92148 h (~11h 55m); Wikipedia and some press materials cite 11h 52min. The Nature paper value is the peer-reviewed measurement.

C2 AUDIT

Claim: "Kinetic-impact deflection experiment established that ANY hazardous asteroid can be made safe regardless of size, structure, or warning time" → OVERGENERALIZATION; NOT SUPPORTED

What DART actually established (per NASA and the four Nature papers of Mar 1, 2023):

  • A kinetic impactor can successfully intercept and strike a small asteroid autonomously NASA Marshall
  • The resulting orbital change far exceeded the 73-second minimum success threshold, by >25× [NASA Release 22-105]
  • Momentum enhancement factor β = 2.2–4.9 (mutual orbit) via ejecta recoil substantially amplified the spacecraft's direct impulse [Cheng et al., Nature 616, 457–460]
  • It serves as a proof-of-concept for the kinetic impactor technique [Chabot et al., Acta Astronautica 2024]

What the evidence does NOT support — the stated limitations:

  1. Warning time is essential, not optional. The orbital change per impact is tiny (mm/s scale for heliocentric deflection). NASA states: "What is necessary is sufficient warning time — several years at a minimum, but preferably decades." With only a couple of decades of warning, the kinetic impactor is "quite sufficient" only for modest trajectory changes; short-warning scenarios are not addressed. NASA Marshall; Space.com analysis

  2. Size matters. DART demonstrated deflection of a ~160-m body. Larger asteroids require proportionally larger momentum transfer — multiple missions or much more massive impactors. The ~140–1000 m size range is where kinetic impact is most practical; below ~30 m, objects fragment in the atmosphere; above several hundred meters, single-impact deflection becomes impractical. Space.com; Rivkin et al., PMC9978022

  3. Structure strongly affects outcome. Dimorphos proved to be a porous rubble-pile (~35% macroporosity, bulk density <2,400 kg/m³, cohesion <50 Pa). The DART impact caused global deformation rather than a conventional crater. Raducan et al., Nature Astronomy 2024. The authors caution: "these findings may not be applicable to single, small, S-type asteroids." Monolithic versus rubble-pile structures produce very different β factors and fragmentation risks. Space.com warns: "It's plausible that you could inadvertently break off a chunk of the asteroid when you hit it rather than just deflecting it as a whole unbroken object. Those fragments would then pose their own threats."

  4. Partial-deflection risk. If the deflection is insufficient to clear Earth but shifts the impact point, it creates a different disaster scenario rather than preventing one. Space.com

  5. Characterization gap. NASA acknowledges: we cannot know an asteroid's mass, shape, composition, or internal structure from Earth alone — "That makes it actually maybe a little more challenging than if you had a longer warning time." Space.com

Corrected statement: DART established that kinetic impact is a viable proof-of-concept for asteroid deflection of a small (~160 m) rubble-pile body, with ejecta-enhanced momentum transfer, when sufficient warning time (years to decades) is available. It does not establish universal applicability to any hazardous asteroid regardless of size, structure, or warning time.

MUTUAL-ORBIT vs HELIOCENTRIC-ORBIT SUMMARY

Quantity Mutual Orbit (Dimorphos around Didymos) Heliocentric Orbit (Didymos-Dimorphos around Sun)
Pre-impact period 11.92148 ± 0.00013 h (~11h 55m) 770 days (~2.1 yr)
Change −33.0 ± 1.0 min (Nature 2023); refined to −33 min 15 s (Mar 2024) −150 ± 20 ms; Δv = −11.7 ± 1.3 μm/s; Δa = −360 ± 40 m
First announced Oct 11, 2022 (~32 min ±2 min) Mar 2026 (Science Advances)
Published Nature 616, 448–451 (Mar 1, 2023) Science Advances 12, 10 (Mar 6, 2026)
Key paper Thomas et al. (2023) Makadia et al. (2026)

These are fundamentally different measurements and must not be conflated.

evidence.snippet: NASA DART mission page: 'On Sept. 26, 2022, DART impacted the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos, a small body just 530 feet (160 meters) in diameter. It orbits a larger, 2,560-foot (780-meter) asteroid called Didymos.' (Paraphrase)

NASA Release 22-105, Oct 11, 2022: 'the investigation team has confirmed the spacecraft's impact altered Dimorphos' orbit around Didymos by 32 minutes, shortening the 11 hour and 55-minute orbit to 11 hours and 23 minutes. This measurement has a margin of uncertainty of approximately plus or minus 2 minutes.' (Paraphrase)
evidence.supports: First announcement was ~32 min ±2 min on Oct 11, 2022, not 33 min 15 s.

evidence.snippet: Thomas et al., Nature 616, 448-451, published Mar 1, 2023: 'Here we report the change in the orbital period of Dimorphos as a result of the DART kinetic impact to be −33.0 ± 1.0 (3σ) min.' Pre-impact 11.92148 ± 0.00013 h; post-impact 11.372 ± 0.017 h. (Paraphrase)
evidence.supports: Peer-reviewed value is −33.0 ± 1.0 min; published Mar 1, 2023.

evidence.snippet: JPL/Naidu et al., Mar 2024: 'Immediately after impact, DART reduced...Dimorphos' orbital period by 32 minutes and 42 seconds...finally settling at 11 hours, 22 minutes, and 3 seconds per orbit – 33 minutes and 15 seconds less time than before impact. This calculation is accurate to within 1½ seconds.' (Paraphrase)
evidence.supports: '33 min 15 s' is the March 2024 refined value, not the first announcement.

evidence.snippet: Makadia et al., Science Advances (2026): 'we estimate that the Didymos system experienced an along-track velocity change of −11.7 ± 1.3 micrometers per second...−360 ± 40m change in the semimajor axis...150 ± 20 ms reduction in the system's 2.1-year orbital period.' (Paraphrase)
evidence.supports: Heliocentric orbit change is ~0.15 s in period / −11.7 μm/s — entirely separate from the ~33-min mutual orbit change.

evidence.snippet: NASA Marshall (Mar 1, 2023): 'What is necessary is sufficient warning time — several years at a minimum, but preferably decades.' (Paraphrase)
evidence.supports: Warning time of years-to-decades is required; kinetic impact is not universally applicable.

evidence.snippet: Space.com analysis of DART limitations: 'When you've got a couple decades' worth of warning time, the kinetic impactor can be quite sufficient'... 'It's plausible that you could inadvertently break off a chunk of the asteroid when you hit it rather than just deflecting it as a whole'... 'That would be useful information that we don't have very much for DART. That makes it actually maybe a little more challenging than if you had a longer warning time.' (Paraphrase)
evidence.supports: Size, structure, and warning time all constrain applicability; no universal claim is justified.

evidence.snippet: Raducan et al., Nature Astronomy (2024): Dimorphos is 'probably more porous and, therefore, may have a rubble-pile structure throughout the whole body' with ~35% macroporosity; 'these findings may not be applicable to single, small, S-type asteroids.' (Paraphrase)
evidence.supports: Target structure critically affects outcome; results do not generalize to all asteroid types.
